entries.clue: Disorderly mess left inside sailing boat (7)

indicatorNotes.inside: What is put inside a thing sits within its letters rather than in front of them or after them.

blocks.note: a cutter is a small single-masted sailing boat, and it opens up after its first letter
l = left, the abbreviation used on maps and in stage directions

annotation.surface: An untidy heap of belongings abandoned on board a small yacht.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Disorderly' opens the clue looking like an instruction to shuffle, and nothing here is shuffled — it is half the definition. A cutter is a working boat with one mast and a long bowsprit.
annotation.definitionFit: Clutter is things strewn about with no order to them, which is a disorderly mess in the plainest sense.

entries.clue: British singer accepting help somewhere in Australia (8)

indicatorNotes.accepting: To accept something is to take it in and keep it, so the letters named next go inside the word that accepted them.

blocks.note: Adele, the Londoner who sings 'Someone Like You', goes by her first name alone
aid is help, and these three letters lodge after the fourth

annotation.surface: A British pop star taking assistance from someone while on tour down under.
annotation.walkthrough: One proper name swallows another, which is why 'British singer' is a person and the answer is a place. The vagueness of 'somewhere' is the setter's, and the crossings settle which somewhere it is.
annotation.definitionFit: Adelaide is the coastal capital of South Australia, so it is one place the definition's 'somewhere' can be.

entries.clue: The chap caught up in tough spot is running late (6)

indicatorNotes.caught up in: To be caught up in something is to be held inside it, and in a down entry 'up' lifts what is held so those letters arrive back to front.

blocks.note: a bind is an awkward fix you cannot easily get out of
the chap is HE, and this entry runs downwards, so he climbs and lands the other way round

annotation.surface: A man tangled in a difficult situation has lost track of the time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Caught up in' reads as the man's predicament and is two instructions at once. There is no backwards on a vertical axis: a down piece told to go up reads from the bottom of the grid towards the top.
annotation.definitionFit: To be behind is to be later than you should be — 'behind with the rent', 'running behind' — which is running late.

entries.clue: King or queen maybe meet comedian (4,4)

blocks.note: to face someone is to meet them head on
a card is British slang for an amusing character: 'he's a proper card'

annotation.surface: A monarch being introduced to a stand-up comic.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' is doing real work: two of the picture cards are named and the answer is the class they belong to. Both halves of the wordplay are ordinary words wearing their second meanings.
annotation.definitionFit: A face card is any of the jack, queen and king, the ones with a face printed on them, so a king is one example.

entries.clue: Somewhat fallow, interminably cold part of the year (6)

indicatorNotes.Somewhat: Somewhat means only part of what follows is wanted, and the part wanted is a run of letters already sitting there in order.

blocks.note: six consecutive letters running across the comma, beginning at the end of the first word

annotation.surface: Ground left unplanted through an endlessly chilly stretch of the year.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Interminably' looks like the instruction to lop the end off a word — without end — and does nothing of the sort; it is simply letters. Nothing is rearranged either: the run reads straight off the page.
annotation.definitionFit: Winter is the coldest of the four seasons, so it is the cold part of the year the definition describes without naming it.

entries.clue: You and I are mostly bored by the rain and snow, perhaps (7)

indicatorNotes.mostly: Most of a word is all of it bar the end, so the final letter is dropped before the piece is used.
indicatorNotes.bored by: To bore into something is to drill through it, so whatever does the boring finishes up inside the word it went through.

blocks.note: the two of us taken together are 'we'
ARE handed over with its final letter dropped
the definite article, taken as its three letters, drilling in after the third

annotation.surface: Two people thoroughly fed up with the rain and snow outside.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bored' is tedium in the surface and drilling in the wordplay, and only the second sense moves any letters. 'Perhaps' flags rain and snow as instances rather than definitions.
annotation.definitionFit: Weather is whatever the sky is doing, and rain and snow are two kinds of it — 'perhaps' marks them as examples standing in for the whole.

entries.clue: Promise of place with slight advantage (6)

blocks.note: pl = place, the abbreviation that appears on street signs
an edge is the narrow lead one side holds over another

annotation.surface: A guarantee of somewhere to live, with a small perk thrown in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Place' is a spot in the surface and two letters in the wordplay, the abbreviation off a sign such as Portland Pl. 'Edge' here is the competitor's advantage, not a border.
annotation.definitionFit: A pledge is a solemn promise, the noun you give rather than the verb you make.

entries.clue: Recital changed to incorporate new instrument (8)

indicatorNotes.changed: What has been changed no longer looks the way it arrived, and for letters that means coming out in a new order.
indicatorNotes.incorporate: To incorporate something is to take it into the body of a thing, so the letter named joins the pool being rearranged.

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder
n = new, the eighth letter joining the shuffle

annotation.surface: A concert programme rewritten so that another player can join in.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder is a music word sitting in a music sentence, which is the hardest sort to notice. Two signals are at work: one shuffles, the other says the extra letter belongs in the mix.
annotation.definitionFit: A clarinet is a woodwind instrument, so the definition simply names the class it belongs to.

entries.clue: Contentious character central to stories in horribly vile cartoons (13)

indicatorNotes.central to: What is central to a word is the single letter sitting exactly in the middle of it, and that letter is all that is taken.
indicatorNotes.horribly: Something done horribly has come out badly wrong, and letters that have gone wrong turn up in the wrong order.

blocks.note: 'character' means a letter here, and STORIES has seven of them, so one of them stands in the middle
twelve more letters of fodder

annotation.surface: A divisive figure at the heart of the news, drawn in some nasty cartoons.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Character' is the public figure of the surface and a single letter in the wordplay, the pivot the whole clue turns on. 'Stories' has an odd number of letters, which is what lets one of them be central.
annotation.definitionFit: Something controversial sets people arguing, and contentious describes the same thing: it provokes dispute wherever it goes.

entries.clue: Stable about to take on one horse (8)

indicatorNotes.to take on: To take somebody on is to take them into your own ranks, so what is taken on ends up inside the letters already assembled rather than after them.

blocks.note: a stall is the stable compartment one animal stands in
on = about: a programme on badgers is a programme about them
the Roman numeral for one, which slips into the join

annotation.surface: A stable with room for one more animal.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word of this quiet little sentence is doing cryptic work, which is what makes it hard. 'Stable' is the building in the surface and the single compartment inside it in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A stallion is an uncastrated male horse, kept for breeding — one kind of the animal the definition names.

entries.clue: Group of houses close to off-licence, say (6)

indicatorNotes.close to: The close of a word is the letter it finishes on, and only that last letter is being asked for.

blocks.note: the final letter of the word — an off-licence is a British shop selling drink to take away
to say something is to state it

annotation.surface: A cluster of houses just round the corner from the local booze shop.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Close to' is nearness in the surface and the last letter in the wordplay. In British use the answer means a development of housing built to one plan, not the land round a country house.
annotation.definitionFit: A British estate is a block of houses put up together as one scheme, which is exactly a group of houses.

entries.clue: Act more recklessly and act in a perplexing manner (8)

blocks.note: to act natural is to be natural, so the verbs swap straight over
the comparative of wild, which is how recklessness behaves

annotation.surface: Advice to throw caution away and leave everybody guessing.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter writes 'act' twice on purpose, once as wordplay and once inside the definition, so the seam falls in the middle of a sentence that reads as one instruction. 'Act natural' means 'be natural', which is the swap.
annotation.definitionFit: To bewilder is to leave somebody baffled, which is to act towards them in a perplexing manner.

entries.clue: A selfish desire? No argument there! (6)

blocks.note: the article taken down as the single letter it is
greed is wanting more than your share

annotation.surface: Somebody owns up to a grasping wish and nobody disputes it.
annotation.walkthrough: The punctuation sells the halves as a musing and a reply, when one is wordplay and the other is the definition. The answer is the word of assent itself, not a description of assenting.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Agreed!' is what you say when you accept a point, which is what 'no argument there' says — both are the concession spoken aloud.

entries.clue: Clear reorganisation of field events (4-7)

indicatorNotes.reorganisation of: A reorganisation keeps everything it started with and puts it somewhere else, which for letters means the same ones in a new order.

blocks.note: eleven letters of fodder — in athletics the jumps and throws, as against the races on the track

annotation.surface: The jumping and throwing programme at an athletics meeting being rearranged.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clear' looks like an instruction to empty something and is the definition standing on its own. Everything after it is fodder and signal, with no second piece to find.
annotation.definitionFit: Something self-evident needs no proving because it is obvious on sight, which is 'clear' in the sense of plain rather than transparent.

entries.clue: Pretty fine engraved artwork (8)

blocks.note: f = fine, the grade stamped on a pencil between HB and H
an etching is the print pulled from a plate bitten with acid

annotation.surface: A delicate picture cut into a metal plate.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pretty fine' reads as one phrase and breaks in the middle, the adjective going one way and the pencil grade the other. Pencils are still marked F for fine.
annotation.definitionFit: Something fetching catches the eye and pleases it — the sense that survives in 'a fetching hat' — which is what pretty means.

entries.clue: Citizen of North America – Latino, possibly (8)

indicatorNotes.possibly: Possibly says the letters offered could come out as something other than the word they spell, so they are free to be moved about.

blocks.note: n = north, as on a compass
a = America, the single-letter abbreviation
six letters reset in a new order

annotation.surface: Someone from the Americas who might have Latin American roots.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash invites you to read 'North America' as one continent and the wordplay takes it as two separate letters. 'Possibly' is the shuffle signal, hiding behind a word that looks like a description of a person.
annotation.definitionFit: A national of a country is one of its citizens — the word newspapers use when they report on 'a French national'.

entries.clue: Token reply (7)

blocks.note: the small disc you push round a board game, a token in the literal sense
the answer you give back when an argument is put to you

annotation.surface: A response offered as a mere gesture.
annotation.walkthrough: Two nouns and nothing else, which is why the clue is only two words long — the surface phrase 'token reply' is a third reading that belongs to neither half. The shop sense, the thing you pay at, is left alone.
annotation.definitionFit: A counter is the plastic disc that stands for a player in a game, a token; and a counter to an argument is the reply that pushes back against it.

entries.clue: Bird taking off around small lake (7)

indicatorNotes.around: What goes around a thing encloses it, so the letters named next sit within this word instead of following it.

blocks.note: a plane taking off is going, and the word splits after its second letter
s = small, the clothing size
l = lake, the abbreviation used on maps before a name

annotation.surface: A bird lifting off and circling a small stretch of water.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Taking off' is the bird's departure in the surface and the flat verb 'going' in the wordplay. The joke underneath is that the answer is a young goose, still in down and unable to fly.
annotation.definitionFit: A gosling is a baby goose, so it answers 'Bird' as one example of the kind.

entries.clue: Little kid suppresses surprising cry as well (2,4)

indicatorNotes.suppresses: To suppress a sound is to keep it in rather than let it out, so the letters named are held inside the word doing the suppressing.

blocks.note: a tot is a small child, and the word opens between its second and third letters
the shout you jump out with to startle somebody, not the jeer

annotation.surface: A small child stifling a shout of surprise.
annotation.walkthrough: 'As well' looks like more of the sentence and is the definition sitting out in the open. 'Surprising' is there to steer the cry away from the theatre, where the same syllable means the opposite.
annotation.definitionFit: 'To boot' means in addition — 'he was rude, and late to boot' — so it drops into the same slot as 'as well'.

entries.clue: No item needing to be recycled promptly (2,4)

indicatorNotes.needing to be recycled: What is recycled is broken up and made into something else out of the same material, which is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder, taken from both words together

annotation.surface: A household with nothing in the bin that has to go out in a hurry.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole surface is about recycling, which is how the one instruction in the clue hides in plain sight. Definition and answer are both adverbial, so one drops straight in for the other.
annotation.definitionFit: To arrive on time is to arrive promptly: both say the appointed moment was met and not missed.

entries.clue: Backlash concerning director’s call? (8)

blocks.note: re = concerning, the heading at the top of a memo
the word a film director shouts to start a take

annotation.surface: Public anger about something a film director said.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s reads as possession and the call is simply the word bellowed on set. 'Re' is the memo heading, crossword shorthand for 'concerning' and a chunk worth owning.
annotation.definitionFit: A backlash is a reaction, specifically an angry one — the definition names the sharper end of the word, which the question mark admits.

entries.clue: Reluctant amateur poet’s output? (6)

blocks.note: a = amateur, the old distinction from a professional
what a poet produces is verse

annotation.surface: The collected efforts of a part-time poet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Poet's output' is one idea in the surface and two pieces in the wordplay, which is why the apostrophe sits where it does. Watch the spelling: this is the word that takes 'to', not the one that means unfavourable.
annotation.definitionFit: To be averse to something is to be unwilling to do it, which is what reluctant means — both take 'to' after them.

entries.clue: Weightlifting move is strenuous to begin with, of course! (6)

indicatorNotes.to begin with: To begin with points at where a word starts, so only its opening letter is taken from it.

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
'natch' is casual British shorthand for 'naturally'

annotation.surface: An exercise that is punishing from the very first repetition, obviously.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Of course!' looks like the setter's throwaway aside and is five of the six letters. The lift itself takes the bar from floor to arm's length overhead in one movement.
annotation.definitionFit: The snatch is one of the two lifts contested in Olympic weightlifting, the single-pull one rather than the clean and jerk.

entries.clue: Reserve money for summer treat (3,5)

blocks.note: ice is coldness of manner, the reserve in an icy greeting
lolly is British slang for cash, of the same vintage as 'bread'

annotation.surface: Putting cash aside for something to enjoy when the hot weather comes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reserve' is a verb in the surface and a noun in the wordplay — froideur, as in 'she met him with ice'. The two slang senses sit next to each other and make a thing children queue for.
annotation.definitionFit: An ice lolly is frozen juice on a stick, what Americans call a popsicle, and the standard British answer to a hot afternoon.

entries.clue: Final destination of reconstructed tramline (8)

indicatorNotes.reconstructed: Something reconstructed is built again out of the material it came from, which for letters means the same ones in a new arrangement.

blocks.note: eight letters of fodder

annotation.surface: The last stop on a rebuilt tram route.
annotation.walkthrough: Surface and answer are about the same thing, which is what makes the shuffle hard to see: a rebuilt tram route genuinely does end somewhere. One instruction, one bag of letters, nothing else to find.
annotation.definitionFit: A terminal is where a route or a journey stops — the airport building, the last station on the line — so it is the final destination itself.

entries.clue: On regular occasions, situations lead to sticky spots (6)

indicatorNotes.On regular occasions: Something taken on regular occasions is taken at a steady interval, here every other letter counting from the first.
indicatorNotes.lead to: The lead of a word is the letter it starts with, so only the front letter of what follows joins in.

blocks.note: every second letter of the word, counting from its first
the opening letter of the word

annotation.surface: Awkward circumstances that keep landing people in trouble.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lead to' reads as consequence and is an instruction to take a first letter, which is the hinge of the clue. A sticky spot in the surface is a predicament; the definition wants the mark on the carpet.
annotation.definitionFit: A stain is a discoloured spot left on cloth or carpet, so the plural 'spots' is a straight swap for it.
